column2: Why can a creatinine within the non-pregnant normal range indicate kidney impairment in pregnancy?
column3: Renal plasma flow and filtration rise early in pregnancy and lower creatinine, so a value normal outside pregnancy may represent impairment.

column2: Why is the uterus displaced to the left during resuscitation in later pregnancy, and what is prepared early if cardiac arrest resuscitation is difficult?
column3: Displacement reduces uterine compression of the aorta and vena cava; if resuscitation is difficult, emergency delivery of the uterine contents is prepared early according to gestation and fundal height.

column2: Why can respiratory failure and anaesthesia deteriorate rapidly in pregnancy?
column3: Oxygen consumption rises and functional residual capacity falls as the diaphragm elevates, shrinking oxygen reserve during apnoea, while airway oedema and aspiration risk increase.

column2: What makes pregnancy hypercoagulable, and what is the trade-off?
column3: Increased clotting factors, reduced fibrinolysis and venous stasis protect against delivery bleeding but raise venous thrombosis risk, especially postpartum and with surgery, immobility, obesity or thrombophilia.

column2: How does inadequate spiral-artery remodelling lead to pre-eclampsia, and why can placental flow be poor despite high maternal pressure?
column3: Inadequate invasion and remodelling cause placental ischaemia and release antiangiogenic and inflammatory signals that injure maternal endothelium, so maternal pressure can be high while placental flow remains poor.

column3: Prolonged vomiting depletes thiamine, and giving substantial carbohydrate first can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

column2: Why can pre-eclampsia be diagnosed without proteinuria?
column3: It is a multisystem placental endothelial disease, so new hypertension after mid-pregnancy with kidney, liver, neurological, haematological, pulmonary or placental dysfunction meets the syndrome.

column2: Why is the newborn of a mother with gestational diabetes at risk of hypoglycaemia after birth?
column3: Maternal glucose crossing the placenta drives fetal insulin; at birth the placental glucose supply stops abruptly while neonatal insulin remains high.

column2: Why is vasa praevia dangerous to the fetus when membranes rupture?
column3: Fetal vessels cross the membranes near the cervix, so membrane rupture can produce catastrophic fetal bleeding.

column2: Why is fetal heart monitoring not read as a direct measure of fetal oxygenation?
column3: It reflects the autonomic response to oxygenation, so baseline, variability, accelerations, decelerations, contractions, gestation, medicines and context are interpreted together.

column2: Why is traction on the fetal head avoided in shoulder dystocia, and what is used instead?
column3: Traction does not release the shoulder and can injure the brachial plexus; maternal positioning, suprapubic pressure, internal rotation or posterior-arm delivery are used, and fundal pressure is avoided.

column2: Why can an apparently mild fall in fibrinogen indicate severe obstetric haemorrhage?
column3: Fibrinogen falls early in obstetric haemorrhage, and because its reference range is higher in pregnancy, a value that looks mildly low may reflect severe disease.

column2: Why should the physiological tachycardia and raised white-cell count of pregnancy not be used to dismiss sepsis?
column3: Fever may not be prominent, so tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, altered consciousness, oliguria and fetal tachycardia are early signs, and change over time and organ function carry more weight.

column2: Why is breastfeeding not automatically stopped when a mother needs a medicine?
column3: Most medicines can be continued; safety depends on milk transfer, infant age, absorption, half-life, toxicity, alternatives and maternal need, and a blanket stop risks an untreated mother or unwanted weaning.
